analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal tax breaks, royalties relief, and financing for coal, oil, and gas production.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2024 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end a long list of federal supports for fossil fuel companies: tax deductions and credits for oil, gas, and coal producers, below-market royalties on public land, limits on oil spill liability, and US-backed financing for fossil fuel projects overseas. It would also raise the excise taxes that fund oil spill cleanup and black lung benefits for coal miners. The goal is to stop taxpayers from effectively subsidizing fossil fuel production.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers would keep money now spent or foregone supporting fossil fuel production. Coal miners would benefit from higher excise taxes funding the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund. Taxpayers and coastal communities would face less risk from offshore spills, since the bill removes liability caps and ends royalty relief for offshore drillers.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates a wide list of tax expenditures for fossil fuel producers, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion for coal and oil shale, capital gains treatment of coal royalties, and the corporate tax exemption for publicly traded fossil fuel partnerships [S2].
Raises the federal royalty rate that companies pay to extract oil, gas, and coal from public land from 12.5% to 18.75%, and bars royalty relief on offshore leases [S2].

Removes the statutory cap on liability for offshore oil spill damages, and makes pipelines carrying heavy Canadian oil (diluted bitumen) fully liable for spills, shifting cleanup risk from taxpayers to the companies [S2].
Increases the excise tax that funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which pays benefits to coal miners disabled by black lung disease [S2].

Prohibits federal agencies and international financing institutions (Export-Import Bank, DFC, USAID and others) from funding fossil fuel projects, and bars the Department of Energy, USDA, and ARPA-E from funding fossil fuel, carbon capture, and non-clean hydrogen projects [S2].

Repeals provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility Act that mandated approval of the Mountain Valley Pipeline and shortened environmental review, and repeals Inflation Reduction Act provisions requiring offshore oil leasing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies would pay higher taxes, higher royalties on public land, full spill liability, and lose access to federal financing and research programs. Energy costs could rise for consumers where producers pass those costs on. Major banks and large lenders would also lose their exemption from cleanup liability under CERCLA when they finance fossil fuel projects.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and large lenders

drawbacks.text: Repealing tax preferences like intangible drilling cost expensing and LIFO accounting would raise production costs for US oil, gas, and coal, and some of that cost would likely be passed through to consumers in energy prices [S2].

The bill terminates the section 45Q carbon capture credit and bars DOE funding for carbon capture and most hydrogen projects, which would end support for technologies both industry and some climate-policy supporters argue are needed for deep emissions cuts [S2].
Removing liability caps and lender exemptions raises legal and financial risk for energy infrastructure, which industry argues deters investment in domestic production and grid reliability [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits—ending taxpayer subsidies, higher royalties on public resources, full polluter liability, and a better-funded black lung trust fund—run mostly to the public, while its costs fall mainly on fossil fuel companies. The honest tradeoff is energy prices: shrinking subsidies and raising royalties could push fuel costs up for consumers, and killing the carbon capture credit sacrifices a technology some climate experts favor. On balance the design is consistent and the costs are concentrated on the industry it targets, but the scale of consumer price impact depends on how much producers pass through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2024, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2024 on May 23, 2024, with six Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies are better off because the bill died: they keep the tax deductions, credits, royalty relief, liability limits, and federal financing the bill would have eliminated. Taxpayers continue to bear those costs.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate fossil fuel subsidies and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Sens. Merkley, Booker, Van Hollen, Welch, Warren, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican joined.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 23, 2024 and never held a markup or moved it out of committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the bill stalled in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would end enhanced oil recovery and marginal well credits, percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost expensing, LIFO accounting, and the corporate tax exemption for fossil fuel partnerships, and raise public-land royalties from 12.5% to 18.75%. Its industry gains are paid for by taxpayers through lower royalties and higher deficits.

The bill repeals percentage depletion for coal, capital gains treatment of coal royalties, the refined coal production credit, and advanced coal project credits, while raising the black lung excise tax on coal. Coal mining's public health costs are currently partly financed by a trust fund the bill would replenish.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel pipelines and offshore drillers
industries.note: The bill removes statutory caps on offshore spill liability, extends full liability to bitumen pipelines, denies tax deductions for spill damages, and mandates a 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico production. Liability caps currently shift cleanup risk from operators to the public.

The bill removes the CERCLA exemption that protects banks over $10 billion in assets and investment firms over $250 billion under management from cleanup liability when they foreclose on contaminated fossil fuel properties. It would not affect smaller community lenders.

The bill terminates the 45Q carbon sequestration credit and bars DOE Loan Programs Office funding for carbon capture and non-clean hydrogen, while narrowing the clean hydrogen credit to projects powered by new renewables in the same region.

industries.industry: Federal export and development finance agencies
industries.note: The bill prohibits the Export-Import Bank, DFC, USAID, TDA, MCC, and US contributions to international financial institutions from funding fossil fuel projects, rescinding equivalent funds if they do. Taxpayer-backed export credit currently underwrites fossil fuel projects abroad.
